rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.5 and 3; the authors run their own SWAP model simulations for a 500 ha district in Northern Italy (2010-2013) using measured canal inflows and bi-weekly piezometer readings, calibrate an empirical percolation-groundwater depth relation (Eq. 7, R2 0.86 calibration, 0.90 validation) and run scenario analyses (Tables 7, 8).
rows.notes: The study does not test drip irrigation at all. It analyses a scenario of switching rice from continuous submergence to flush irrigation (intermittent 150 mm flushes scheduled on demand in SWAP), with maize under border irrigation and poplars. Its finding (Section 3.3.2, Table 7, Conclusions) is that, when the feedback between reduced percolation and groundwater depth is accounted for, flush irrigation lowers summer groundwater by about 35 cm and raises maize irrigation requirements by about 50% (15-day to 10-day turn), so district withdrawal reduction drops from ~80% to ~60%. This matches the effect in the passage but for flush irrigation, not drip; the scenario outputs themselves are model predictions not checked against measurements of the modified system. Technology mismatch therefore Q2 = no and Q3-Q9 = no. For the record, the study does state support factors (highly permeable soils, shallow groundwater; Conclusions), limitations (empirical relation valid only within calibrated percolation range; yield gaps, nutrients and ecosystem services not addressed; Section 3.2 and Conclusions) and standard deviations across years (Tables 7, 8), but these relate to flush irrigation.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a district-scale model-based scenario analysis of flush irrigation of rice in a shallow-groundwater district; the review attributes its finding to drip irrigation, which the study never considers.
